seo.title: Which Is Better OEM or ODM? A Swimwear Buyer's Guide
seo.description: Compare OEM and ODM swimwear using launch costs, fit evidence, delivery milestones, and file ownership to choose the right route for your US brand.

title: Which is better, OEM or ODM?
lead: For a US swimwear brand, OEM is usually better when distinctive fit or construction is essential and you can support custom development. ODM is usually better when an existing design meets your brief and you want to reduce development work. Compare the actual samples, launch cash, delivery plan, and file handover before choosing; the manufacturing label alone does not settle those questions. The general tradeoff is explained in [SEACOMP's OEM vs ODM manufacturing guide](https://www.seacomp.com/resources/oem-vs-odm-manufacturing).

At Strandmill, we work from your design, a reference picture, or an idea, and we also offer ready designs. Your starting point should be the product promise: what must a customer feel, see, or experience that a standard style cannot already deliver?

image.alt: Designer examining a swimwear sample at a development table

sections.heading: Choosing OEM or ODM for your swimwear launch

body.text: Choose OEM if the fit or construction you need goes beyond what a ready style can demonstrate. Choose ODM if a tested existing style meets your brief and the quoted cash requirement and schedule work for you. Neither route automatically means lower minimums, a cheaper delivered order, or production files you can take elsewhere.
Start with a physical sample alongside your design brief. Check the silhouette, coverage, lining, and support before deciding how much development your design needs.

Here, OEM means making a buyer-defined design, while ODM means manufacturer-led design, often based on an existing style. OEM gives you more room to develop something distinctive; an existing ODM design can cut development spending and time. [Brightpearl's OEM vs ODM guide](https://www.brightpearl.com/blog/oem-vs-odm-explained) explains the distinction. Suppliers use these terms differently, so ask who develops the pattern, who approves changes, and exactly what the proposal covers.

body.subheading: Compare launch cash on the same basis

body.text: Ask for each proposal to use the same fabric, lining, size mix, quality requirements, packaging, and US delivery address. Keep garment prices separate from development, sample courier charges, freight, and import costs. A smaller sample bill only helps if the rest of the order still works within your budget.

Our starting minimum is 50 pieces per style in each color, spread across 3 to 4 sizes. Your fabric and print choices can change the exact minimum. A bikini top and matching bottom count as one piece when you order them as a set; tops and bottoms sold separately count separately. Put that unit definition into your comparison before multiplying the quantities.

We charge USD 50 per design, covering its pattern or print across colorways, along with the tech pack and CAD pattern we prepare. Each physical sample costs USD 50, and each revised fit sample is charged as a new sample. Sample courier delivery costs USD 50. These fees are not credited against bulk. Minor digital adjustments are free, and we remake a sample without charge if it differs significantly from the approved handover. Our [Development page](/development/) can help you prepare the sampling scope.

For this worked budget, assume a solid-color swimsuit with the same nylon-spandex fabric and lining, the same S/M/L size mix, and standard packing. There is no new print, hardware, or separate lab testing. Assume 100 garments at USD 18 each for OEM and 100 garments at USD 19 each for ODM. These garment prices and logistics allowances are assumed inputs, not Strandmill quotations. Both routes include a charged design. OEM needs an initial sample and a revised fit sample, shipped separately; ODM needs only an initial sample and courier shipment.

In this example, you spend USD 250 on samples and design for OEM, compared with USD 150 for ODM. Our 50% garment deposit comes to USD 900 for OEM and USD 950 for ODM, bringing the cash committed through bulk booking to USD 1,150 and USD 1,100 respectively. The remaining garment balances of USD 900 and USD 950 are due before shipment. With the assumed logistics costs paid before sale, either route requires USD 2,600 before you sell any stock.

This covers your inventory, not your whole business launch. Keep photography, store, advertising, storage, and your returns reserve outside this budget, then include them in your business cash plan. When calculating the total order cost, do not count the deposit twice.

If the assumed garment prices and logistics allowances stay the same, an order of 50 garments brings the OEM total to USD 1,700 and the ODM total to USD 1,650. At 200 garments, the totals become USD 4,400 for OEM and USD 4,500 for ODM. This calculation shows how development spending can have more influence at smaller quantities, while a lower garment price can have more influence at larger quantities.

Get fresh prices for each quantity rather than treating these assumptions as a volume quote. Ask for minimums by style, color, and size allocation, plus separate accessory minimums where they apply. For a delivered proposal, check which freight, duty, and clearance costs are included, and keep the supporting breakdown. Our DDP option covers delivery to your door, and we handle duties, customs, and freight through our forwarding partners, so do not add those charges again. You can find order and shipping questions in our [FAQ](/faq/).

body.subheading: Find the boundary of a ready style's fit

body.text: Approve print changes separately from fit changes. Keep a change log that records the request, its effect on the pattern, the sample outcome, and final approval. [JLCCNC's OEM vs ODM comparison](https://jlccnc.com/blog/oem-vs-odm) explains the general principle that modifications depend on the existing platform, but your swimwear decisions still need evidence from the garment.

In our anonymized long-torso swimsuit review, the buyer's logo placement worked on a ready style without changing the pattern. A firmer lining changed how the leg opening felt, while the requested torso length and fuller front coverage needed a revised body pattern and regrading. The buyer chose custom development because the ready silhouette did not provide the intended fit.

Look inside the garment as well as at its outside shape. On a supported swimsuit, you can compare visible details such as the lining attachment and underbust elastic before requesting a different level of support.

figure.alt: Inside of a swimsuit showing the lining attachment and underbust elastic
figure.caption: Look inside at the lining and underbust elastic

body.text: The pattern-maker's final change log for that review recorded the outcomes below. The measurements are for the finished garment laid flat, using the buyer's agreed front-body measurement from shoulder seam to crotch seam.

rows: Digital placement changed; body pattern retained
Leg opening reshaped; lining edge revised; additional fit sample required
No visible show-through under the agreed wet-and-stretched check; lining recovered without visible bagging; underbust stayed seated during arm raises
Accept final revision for this brief

body.text: These results apply to that particular style, fabric, and revision. For your range, record the wearer's fit comments alongside the measurements, and repeat the check wherever coverage or support changes between sizes. A photograph can show you the lining and seam placement, but it cannot establish stretch recovery or support on its own.

We fit the base size to your measurement sheet and wear-test it wet for stretch, coverage, and opacity before grading the range. For light colors, we check wet opacity again on the finished garment under stretch before bulk approval. Our fabric and trim reports cover the materials actually tested. We can arrange order-specific laboratory reports at your cost. Use our [One Piece Swimsuit Manufacturer page](/one-piece-swimsuit-manufacturer/) to define your product brief and our [Custom Swimwear Printing page](/custom-swimwear-printing/) for your artwork needs.

An existing design can shorten development, but the time saved depends on fabric availability and how quickly approvals happen. [SEACOMP's manufacturing comparison](https://www.seacomp.com/resources/oem-vs-odm-manufacturing) explains this general speed advantage. To make a useful booking decision, you need a project schedule that also accounts for your waiting time and delivery.

Our standard sample takes 10 to 15 days. Bulk production usually takes 35 to 40 days after sample approval and receipt of your deposit, depending on quantity and season. Allow an extra 2 to 3 weeks for a new mold or print. These production windows do not cover the full journey to your US receiving address.

Both anonymized OEM and ODM project logs below started with a complete handover on 2026-03-02 and used available solid-color fabric. The OEM buyer asked for a fit revision, while the ODM buyer kept the existing pattern. Both projects used air delivery, and neither needed a new print or mold.

rows: Fabric, packing, deposit, and production booking confirmed

body.text: Build your planner around complete handover, sample approval, material readiness, production booking, bulk and inspection, and US delivery. Assign an owner and a confirmed date to each milestone. Show buyer review and sample transport separately rather than burying them within a factory lead time.

chart.alt: Milestone planner from complete handover to US delivery
chart.caption: Assign an owner and date to each launch milestone

body.text: Start with the date your warehouse needs to receive stock and work backward. Reserve receiving time, then allow for freight and clearance, inspection, bulk production, and approvals. Check that the fabric is physically available and the production slot is secured. A ready style can lose its expected head start while waiting for special fabric. If you request a fit change after approval, get a revised schedule before committing to your launch date.

body.subheading: Check what you can take to another factory

body.text: Ask separately about ownership, access, and usable file formats. [inFlow's OEM vs ODM guide](https://www.inflowinventory.com/blog/difference-between-oem-vs-odm/) explains the difference between existing background IP and newly developed foreground IP. Rather than relying on the word “custom,” ask for an inventory of what you will actually receive, including the approved revision.

Our ready-to-go styles stay available to other buyers, but we use the prints, artwork, and branding you add only for you. Custom and ODM designs developed for your brand are exclusive to you. For fully custom projects, the tech packs, CAD patterns, and digitized files we deliver become yours once you pay the related fees. We keep copies for your reorders and do not use them for other clients.

rows: Used only for your brand on our ready styles
Original files, production adaptations, and your rights-holder permissions
Ready style remains in the shared range
Whether any underlying block is included; do not infer release from branding exclusivity
Fully custom pattern and tech pack
Delivered files are yours after related fees are paid
CAD format, approved revision, and measurement specification
Specify the files included in your custom delivery
Size list, grade rules, export format, and opening check
Identify changes incorporated into your delivered design
Separate project changes from pre-existing factory methods

body.text: Our redacted custom handover inventory listed the approved tech pack as PDF, the final pattern as DXF, a graded nest as DXF, and the measurement sheet as XLSX. The release record confirmed paid development fees and permission to produce at another factory, while excluding the unrelated ready-style library. That project had no separate file-transfer charge. Factory changes included in the delivered custom pattern went with the pattern; general sewing methods stayed outside the asset package.

Have the receiving factory open the files and check the size range, seam allowances, and revision against the approved garment. Exclusivity tells you who may use the design; a file inventory tells you what another factory can work with. For your own project, confirm the territory, duration, permitted reuse, release conditions, and any transfer charge in writing. Read our [Terms and Conditions](/terms-and-conditions/) alongside your project-specific agreement.

body.subheading: Make the decision from the evidence

body.text: Choose your development route using the completed comparison. If a deciding factor is still unresolved, get the evidence you need before placing your bulk order.

rows: Ready samples cannot deliver the required fit
Custom development and delivered inventory fit the budget
Existing-design proposal fits the available cash
Materials and approvals preserve the time advantage
Your advantage needs a custom design and usable files

sections.heading: Compare OEM and ODM against one swimwear brief

body.text: Use the same collection brief for both proposals. Include your intended customer, fit and support needs, fabric and lining, size range, style and color quantities, cash budget, and required US delivery date. Attach reference garments or a measurement sheet so the sample team can evaluate what “better fit” means for you.

Ask for sample evidence, a dated milestone plan, a delivered-cost breakdown, and written file-handover terms with each proposal. Start the comparison through our [Request a Quote page](/request-a-quote/). Choose the route that meets your brief with approved samples and a delivery plan you can afford.

seo.title: How Much to Start a Clothing Line? Budget Your Launch
seo.description: Compare clothing line startup costs, then work through a swimwear budget covering samples, inventory, cash flow, reorders, and break-even sales.

title: How much money do you need to start a clothing line?
lead: To start a clothing line, you need enough cash to develop your products, get inventory delivered, launch sales, and pay the bills until customer receipts can fund operations and replenishment. For a sense of scale, [Erply's 2025 guide to clothing line startup costs](https://erply.com/how-much-does-it-cost-to-start-a-clothing-line-complete-2025-guide) budgets **$5,000–$15,000** for print-on-demand or dropshipping with basic branding and limited marketing, and **$15,000–$50,000** for small-batch production with professional branding and a comprehensive marketing launch.

image.alt: Designer examining a navy bikini sample at a worktable

sections.heading: Your clothing line startup budget, broken down

body.text: Pick your production route before you pick a savings target. Those published budgets describe different kinds of businesses, and your own target comes from the products, services, and payment dates in your plan. Below, we'll walk through a swimwear collection from its sample charges to its first reorder, keeping the same assumptions all the way through.

rows: Artwork, product checks, store setup, and customer acquisition; inventory investment is limited
Does an available product suit your idea?
Selected inventory, branding, delivery, and selling costs
Can the existing fit and available assortment serve your customer?
Design, physical samples, revisions, production, delivery, and selling costs
Is a distinct fit or construction essential to the offer?

body.text: The route comparison follows [Erply's 2025 guide to clothing line startup costs](https://erply.com/how-much-does-it-cost-to-start-a-clothing-line-complete-2025-guide). Collection size and how you sell also shape the budget. An online launch still needs selling infrastructure and marketing, as [VistaPrint's How Much Does It Cost to Start a Clothing Brand?](https://www.vistaprint.com/hub/how-much-does-it-cost-to-start-a-clothing-brand) explains.

For swimwear, start by deciding whether an existing silhouette gives your customer the coverage and support they need. Branding can personalize a ready design, but changing the fit can mean new development. We offer both existing designs and custom development. To define the product you'd like priced, [see our Bikini Manufacturer page](/bikini-manufacturer/).

body.subheading: Build the launch ledger around a specific collection

body.text: Give every expense its own place in the ledger, and keep the specification right beside it: fabric, lining, hardware, branding, packing, quantities by size, destination, and delivery terms. Compare the original estimate with the final payment or remaining allowance, and note why it changed. That makes it easier to tell whether a lower quote is a real saving or a different product.

Our worked example assumes a US direct-to-consumer swimwear launch. It applies our development fees and production payment terms to assumed garment prices, delivery charges, independent service costs, and sales. Use its structure to build your own budget, swapping the planning inputs for your itemized quotes.

Say the order is confirmed on April 13, 2026: 150 navy triangle tops at $12 each and 150 matching bottoms at $8 each. They sell as separates, and the sales model groups them into 150 paired purchases. The specification uses standard nylon-spandex fabric, matching lining, standard unbranded hardware, and plain individual bags. Outer presentation packaging comes from an independent supplier and gets its own budget line. All amounts are in USD.

rows: Assumed paid; shipment-specific amount, not a tariff rate
Assumed paid; buyer requested another fit sample

body.text: The assumed factory garment bill is $3,000. Outer packaging brings the inventory subtotal to $3,300, and freight and clearance bring delivered inventory to $4,200. Development and other launch expenses add $2,600, so full launch spending comes to **$6,800** against an original estimate of $6,500. The $300 increase breaks down as $100 more for packaging, $100 for sampling, and $50 each for freight and clearance.

This launch subtotal stops once the collection is ready to sell. Recurring software, fulfillment, customer acquisition, refunds, and replenishment go into the cash calendar or the sale calculation below. Founder living costs are a separate decision. Keep the import allowance tied to the shipment, and replace it with the applicable bill once you have it.

We offer FOB, CIF, and DDP shipping terms. With DDP, our all-in delivery price covers freight, duties, and customs to your door. Read the inclusions before you move a quote into your worksheet. If delivery charges are already included, enter that delivered price and don't add the same freight and clearance costs a second time.

body.subheading: Fund sampling through final fit approval

body.text: Our **$50 design fee per design** covers its pattern or print in all colorways, including the tech pack and CAD pattern we prepare. Each physical sample costs **$50**, plus **$50 for sample courier delivery**. These charges aren't refunded or credited against bulk production. Physical fit revisions you request are chargeable, while minor digital adjustments are free. If a sample differs significantly from the approved handover, we remake it at no charge. For what's included, [see our Development page](/development/).

Write your fit brief before you pay for samples, covering intended coverage, support, measurements, fabric, lining, and movement. We assess fit against the measurement sheet and check wet stretch, coverage, and opacity before grading. In the assumed development log below, the buyer changes the coverage brief after the initial samples. Recording that reason explains why the revision is charged.

rows: Separate top and bottom designs; standard fabric and lining
March 16 to 23, 2026: initial samples ready, delivered, and reviewed
Top stays seated during arm raises; bottom meets the brief, but buyer requests more rear coverage
$100 for samples and $100 for separate courier deliveries
April 3 to 10, 2026: revised bottom ready, delivered, and reviewed
Added coverage accepted; no visible show-through during the assumed wet-and-stretched review; no visible lining bagging after release
$50 for a revised sample and $50 courier
Buyer approves the revised bottom and unchanged top; no factory correction required

body.text: The assumed development period runs from March 2 through April 10, 2026, with $400 spent on design, samples, and courier deliveries. If you want room for one more buyer-requested physical revision with its own courier shipment, hold another $100. That reserve stays unspent in the base plan and sits outside the $6,800 launch total.

Keep the approval evidence with the expense record: the measurement sheet, dry and wet fit photographs, the requested change, and the final written approval. Compare the same garment areas under similar conditions so you can see what improved. If your product needs independent laboratory testing, add the quoted fee and time to the plan before you commit to production.

Check the lining and edge seams as part of that review. Look at how the layers meet, how the seam feels under stretch, and whether the lining settles back into place after release. These details tell you whether the sample is ready to become the production reference.

figure.alt: Hands examining the lining and edge seam of a bikini bottom
figure.caption: Look at the lining and edge construction

body.subheading: Price the assortment by style, color, and size

body.text: Our starting minimum is **50 pieces per style in each color**, split across **3 to 4 sizes**, usually in an S:M:L:XL ratio of **1:2:2:1**. The exact minimum depends on your fabric and print choices. A bikini top supplied with its bottom counts as one piece, while tops and bottoms ordered as separates count separately.

The worksheet orders separates and assumes the size allocation shown. Put the accepted allocation on the purchase order, along with the style/color minimum and any fabric or trim minimum. Confirm any total-order requirement while you're getting quotes. For more on ordering, [see our FAQ](/faq/).

This assumed order contains 300 garments, forming 150 same-size pairs with no unmatched opening stock. Each style is above our 50-piece starting minimum in its color. That pairing capacity depends on the allocation, though. If customers choose different sizes for tops and bottoms, some sizes can run short even when total garment quantities match.

To add a color, assume another 60 tops and 60 bottoms, each allocated S/M/L/XL as 10/20/20/10. At the same garment prices, inventory goes up by $1,200. A sample of each garment with separate courier deliveries adds $200, which brings the added commitment to $1,400 before extra packaging and delivery. Adding a colorway to these existing designs carries no new design fee.

To add a navy top style instead, assume 60 tops at $12, allocated 10/20/20/10. That adds $720 of inventory and $150 for design, a sample, and its courier delivery, for $870 before packaging and delivery. If you keep the original bottoms, paired purchases stop at 150, and 60 tops are left unmatched if everyone buys a pair.

Use these comparisons when you trim the collection to fit your cash. Adding a color repeats the commitment across matching garments. Adding a top gives customers another choice but draws on the same bottom inventory. Separates can sell independently, so base your buying plan on how you expect customers to shop.

body.subheading: Schedule cash payments through the first reorder

body.text: Our production payment terms are **50% at order confirmation and 50% before shipment**. Standard samples are ready in **10 to 15 days**. Bulk production usually takes **35 to 40 days** after sample approval and receipt of the deposit, depending on order size and season. Repeats of approved styles skip sampling and use the same bulk window. Put the deposit and balance for both orders in your calendar.

Our photography, branding, and store services are quoted and invoiced separately from production, with half paid when you book and half on delivery of the finished work. This example uses independent-provider costs and assumes they're paid before launch. If we supply those services, use their separate quotes and payment milestones. [See our Swimwear Launch Services page](/swimwear-launch-services/).

The assumed calendar covers March 2 through August 31, 2026, including a repeat order identical to the first. Overhead is $200 a month from April through August. Base sales are 60 paired purchases in June, 30 in July, and 30 in August. Each leaves $68 after variable selling outflows, with cleared payouts available at month-end. The sale calculation below shows how that receipt is built up.

Read the cumulative deficit as the cash you, as the founder, have to put in after each event. We assume overhead and supplier bills leave the account before that month's sales payout arrives. Refunds and other variable selling costs are already deducted from the receipts. Keeping payments and receipts in this order reveals a shortfall that monthly net totals could hide.

rows: April: revised sample, order deposit, launch services and setup, overhead
May 25: balance, packaging, freight, clearance, May overhead
June 1: overhead before delivery and sales
July 15: reorder deposit and July overhead
August 25: reorder balance, packaging, delivery charges, August overhead

body.text: Assume the first order arrives June 2 and the repeat arrives August 31, 2026. The model includes no sales from the repeat stock. Total payments are $12,000: $6,800 for launch, $1,000 in overhead, and $4,200 for delivered reorder inventory. Base receipts total $8,160. The largest deficit is **$7,400 on June 1**, and the deficit left at the end is $3,840.

Add any founder draw on the dates you plan to take it, then recalculate the largest deficit. Treat an emergency reserve as available cash until it's spent. When you use it, record the actual payment in the calendar. Counting both the reserve and that payment as expenses would inflate your funding requirement.

body.subheading: Check how slower sales and delayed delivery change the target

body.text: Test the same collection against different receipt schedules. These assumed scenarios keep the reorder and overhead commitments unchanged. They show the cash you'd need if you go ahead with that replenishment plan despite slower sales. If you decide to postpone or reduce the reorder, that needs its own revised calendar.

Slow sales raise the assumed peak funding need by $1,880 over the base case, and delayed delivery raises it by $2,560. The scenarios keep the same refund allowance and other variable costs per purchase. Covering the highest modeled deficit of $9,960 plus the optional $100 sampling reserve gives you a savings target of **$10,060**, before founder living costs.

chart.alt: Peak cash requirements for the base, slow-sales, and delivery-delay scenarios
chart.caption: Peak cash needed before sales replenish the account

body.text: The delayed-delivery case shifts stock availability and customer receipts but leaves supplier payments where they are. Add extra freight, storage, or refunds if your revised plan incurs them. If a production delay also changes the balance payment date, move that payment too. A useful stress test follows what actually changes in the order and sales schedule.

body.subheading: Calculate both break-even sales and cash recovery

body.text: Contribution measures what each sale leaves after product cost and variable selling expenses. You reach operating break-even when that contribution covers fixed expenses. Cash recovery asks a different question: have cleared receipts paid back the money you've already spent, including inventory still waiting to sell? Use the same order and selling assumptions to calculate each one.

Assume a paired retail purchase of $100. Allow $5 for markdowns and $5 for refunds, then deduct $3 in payment fees, $7 for fulfillment and outbound shipping, $10 for customer acquisition, and $2 for defect-related service. That leaves **$68 per paired purchase before product cost**. Delivered inventory costs $4,200 across 150 pairs, or $28 per pair, which leaves **$40 contribution per paired sale**.

The refund allowance assumes refunded goods bring in no resale proceeds during the modeled period. Defect-related service costs also get no assumed reimbursement from the supplier. If your actual refunds leave the account separately from payouts, give them their own calendar entries and adjust net receipts to match. Keep fixed launch creative separate from the advertising cost assigned to each purchase.

In this example, launch-only operating break-even is $2,600 in fixed expenses divided by $40 contribution, or **65 paired sales**. Add the modeled $1,000 overhead and fixed expenses reach $3,600, which takes **90 paired sales**. Product cost enters this calculation only as the related garments sell.

Recovering the launch cash and overhead takes $7,800 divided by $68 in net receipts, rounded up to **115 paired sales**. At 120 paired sales, receipts of $8,160 exceed that initial spending by $360. At 90 paired sales, receipts are $6,120 and $1,680 is still unrecovered, even though the model has reached operating break-even.

Once the repeat order is fully paid, the cash you've committed rises to $12,000. Recovering it at $68 per paired purchase takes **177 paired sales**. The first collection has only 150 pairs, so selling all of it still leaves $1,800 unrecovered. Under these assumptions, sales from the reorder have to close that gap.

For cash recovery, count the inventory payment when it leaves your account, and use sales receipts before product cost. Deducting product cost again would count the purchase twice. For contribution, assign product cost to each sale even though the supplier has already been paid. Keeping the two apart lets you judge both your margin and the cash available for replenishment.

body.subheading: Compare the collection with the cash you can commit

body.text: The fees, minimum-order rules, and production terms above are our terms. The collection, garment prices, outside services, calendar, and sales are assumed inputs, and the totals follow from them. Read across the decision table before you commit. The assortment determines inventory, development protects approval, and the stressed cash requirement sets the savings you need to carry the plan through replenishment.

rows: Keep the opening collection focused before adding variants
$3,000 factory garments; $4,200 delivered inventory; $6,800 full launch
Compare quotes at the same scope
Compare available savings with the stressed requirement
Feasible within the first order only if sell-through supports it
Requires sales beyond the first collection

sections.heading: Set your clothing line budget before placing an order

body.text: Set your clothing line budget by comparing the cash you have available with the largest modeled shortfall through the first reorder. If the plan doesn't fit, scale back the assortment, reconsider the production route, or revise the launch and reorder schedule before you commit.

Bring a product brief that names your styles, fabric, colors, sizes, quantities, delivery destination, and intended launch timing. Ask for itemized development, garment, branding, packing, and delivery costs, then attach payment dates to the quote. Keep your website, photography, marketing, and living-cost needs in view alongside it.

A factory quote gives you part of the answer. Your budget is complete when the collection can be developed, delivered, sold, and replenished without relying on sales cash that hasn't cleared yet. Bring your brief and proposed assortment to our [Request a Quote](/request-a-quote/) page so we can define the production side of that plan.

seo.title: What Is a Tech Pack? A Swimwear Brand's Guide
seo.description: Learn what a tech pack includes, how it differs from a sewing pattern, and how to review swimwear specifications, sample costs, and approvals.

title: What Is a Tech Pack?
lead: A tech pack, short for technical package, is the instruction document a clothing manufacturer uses to develop and make a garment. It brings together drawings, materials, measurements, construction details and revisions so the brand and factory can work from the same specifications. See [UpHance's guide to creating a fashion tech pack](https://uphance.com/blog/how-to-create-fashion-tech-pack/).

For a swimwear brand, the practical question is whether those instructions describe the suit you want well enough to quote, sample and approve. A beautiful sketch cannot settle how a lining behaves when wet or where a leg opening should sit. Those decisions need technical development and a physical sample.

image.alt: Designer examining a solid navy scoop-back swimsuit at a development table

sections.heading: What a tech pack tells your clothing manufacturer

body.text: A tech pack tells your manufacturer what to make and how to check it. It helps with quoting and sampling, but the measurement sheet inside it doesn't replace the separate sewing pattern; [Techpacker's explanation of a tech pack](https://techpacker.com/blog/tech-packs/what-is-a-tech-pack/) covers this well.

Picture a scoop-back swimsuit with a lined body and elasticated openings. Its silhouette goes in the drawings, its component choices in the materials list, and its finished dimensions in the measurement sheet. The document map below keeps those jobs apart.

rows: Intended customer, coverage, look and use
Where and how to measure the finished garment
Shapes used to cut the garment components
Whether the finished suit feels right
Instructions for future production unless recorded

body.text: At Strandmill, you can start with sketches, reference images or a garment. You decide the intended coverage, customer, color, size range and quantity, and our team works out the patterns, sizing and construction with you. We quote before sampling, and you approve the sample before bulk production goes ahead with the deposit. If you'd like help turning a reference into specifications, have a look at our [Development](/development/) page.

Our scoop-back development case started with a founder's front and back references, a request for fuller seat coverage, and a solid navy color. The handover left out the lining edge treatment, so on the sample the lining rolled into view at the leg opening. We corrected the construction callout and lining pattern, then checked the replacement sample wet and dry. That was a specification omission, and it's separate from the buyer's later request to adjust coverage.

Treat quotation assumptions as questions you need to close: Is the lining full-body? Are the straps adjustable? Is the logo printed or sewn on? A proposed answer can support an estimate, but the sampling handover needs an instruction you've both agreed.

On fully custom projects, the tech packs and CAD patterns we deliver are yours once the related fees are paid. Agree the editable formats and file inventory at the start. Owning a custom pattern doesn't mean the measurement table itself can be used for cutting.

sections.heading: What should a tech pack include?

body.text: A tech pack should hold garment drawings, a bill of materials, measurements, construction instructions, color and artwork references, labels, packaging and revisions. You'll find these core contents in [Shopify's guide to creating a tech pack](https://www.shopify.com/blog/how-to-create-a-tech-pack). Swimwear also needs clear instructions for the shell, lining, elastic and fit.
Use this readiness worksheet to tell provisional quote information apart from approved production information. Give each open field to a person instead of leaving a blank nobody owns.

rows: Agreed front, back and inside views
Factory proposes; brand signs swatches and sample
Patternmaker develops; brand signs measurement sheet
Seam, edge and attachment instructions agreed
Brand supplies artwork; factory checks application
Brand approves files and packing reference
Named document owner keeps approval record

body.text: Body measurements describe the wearer, while finished-garment measurements describe the suit. Beside each point of measure, write the unit, the endpoints, whether it's relaxed or stretched, and the adjustable-strap setting. A stretched measurement also needs an agreed method so that different reviewers don't pull with different force.
Our long-torso review gives you a finished-garment example: front-body length was measured flat from the shoulder seam to the crotch seam. These values belong to that style, not to every swimsuit.

Our body-measurement tolerance is ±1 cm, and straps, bindings and measurements under 10 cm have a ±0.5 cm tolerance. The target progression above applies only to that reviewed style. A fit review still has to check coverage, movement and wet behavior, because passing the measurement check doesn't automatically mean the fit is approved.

For that scoop-back style, we used SHELL-NAVY, LINING-SOFT and ELASTIC-LEG as component references. The inside drawing tied LINING-SOFT to a turned, secured leg edge and ELASTIC-LEG to the enclosed opening. A firmer lining trial pulled against the shell during movement, so the approved combination kept the softer lining and the revised edge construction.

figure.alt: Inside of a navy swimsuit showing lining attachment at the leg opening
figure.caption: Look at the lining attachment inside the leg opening

body.text: Keep physical swatches with the component references. If you need help choosing the shell and a matching lining, see our [Swimwear Fabrics & Sourcing](/swimwear-fabrics-sourcing/) page.

Round off the handover inventory with the approved PDF, editable source, artwork, base pattern, graded pattern files and physical reference. Our redacted custom handover included a PDF pack, a DXF pattern and graded nest, and an XLSX measurement sheet. Give creation to the technical or artwork owner, approval to the brand, and delivery to the named project contact. Then confirm the actual formats for your project.

sections.heading: How much do tech packs cost?

body.text: At Strandmill, the tech pack and CAD pattern we prepare come included in our USD 50 per-design fee, while physical samples and courier delivery cost extra. To budget all the way through sample approval, compare each provider on the same garment, deliverables and revision scope, and ask whether bikini tops and bottoms are counted separately.

Our design fee covers that design's pattern or print in every colorway, and grading and minor digital adjustments are free. Each physical sample is USD 50, plus USD 50 for courier delivery, and a revised fit sample is charged as a new sample. Design, sample and courier fees aren't refunded or credited against bulk orders.

Each of the completed projects below covered a single swimsuit in S/M/L with no print artwork. Both delivered a tech pack, CAD pattern and graded sizing. The totals cover development up to the stated approval and leave out bulk production. These are examples from our projects, not market averages.

columns: Starting inputs and paid sample scope
rows: Founder references; solid fabric; initial sample and lining-edge correction through construction approval; later coverage change excluded
Measurement chart and cup references; stock hardware; initial sample, cup-fit revision and strap refinement through fit approval; custom hardware excluded

body.text: The structured style's extra sampling pushed up its total, but its design fee stayed the same. When you get a quote, write the starting materials, intended sizes, artwork and approval endpoint next to the price. A construction-approved sample and a fully approved fit can involve different amounts of work.

For a like-for-like budget, picture a solid-color scoop-back in S/M/L with an initial sample and a buyer-requested fit revision, each shipped separately to the US. We'll also assume the independent designer's pack and patterns are accepted for sampling without an extra factory preparation charge. Every outside-provider amount below is an assumed input, and the Strandmill column applies our fees to that same assumed scope.

This budget assumes every listed charge is paid by sample approval, and it leaves out bulk production and import duties. Before you commission work, confirm the actual payment dates for documentation, samples and delivery. If you add print artwork, budget separately for physical strike-offs and printed fabric, which we charge per motif. Any credit another provider offers against a later order goes below the cash total, because it doesn't fund development upfront.

chart.alt: Comparison of assumed cash paid through sample approval
chart.caption: Cash through approval under the stated assumptions

body.text: On fully custom projects, the tech packs and CAD patterns we deliver are yours once the related fees are paid. When you're comparing quotes, agree the editable formats and handover inventory so your budget covers the files you need.

In our scoop-back case, the missing lining-edge instruction led to a paid repeat sample and courier charge totaling USD 100. That sample had followed an incomplete handover. The buyer's later coverage change was separate, so it's left out of that rework total.

Now suppose a more complete independent pack costs an extra USD 100. It breaks even only if it prevents the whole USD 100 paid repeat, and avoiding a free digital adjustment recovers none of that fee. The calculation shows the saving you'd need, not a guaranteed outcome.

If a sample differs significantly from our approved handover, we'll remake it at no charge. When you review paid rework, keep that remedy separate from missing instructions and buyer-requested fit changes.

Before you send the pack, make sure the measurements match across the drawings, spreadsheets and exported PDF. As [Techpacker's What Is a Tech Pack? The Complete Fashion Guide](https://techpacker.com/blog/tech-packs/what-is-a-tech-pack/) explains, a missed update can leave conflicting measurements. Fix those inconsistencies before you pay for the next sample, but keep physical fit review in the budget.

sections.heading: How do I make my own tech pack?

body.text: Begin with your style brief. Then add annotated drawings, a materials list, measurement and construction pages, color or artwork instructions, and a revision log. Flag any choices that are still open for technical review, and update the pack once you've sampled. [Techpacker's What Is a Tech Pack? The Complete Fashion Guide](https://techpacker.com/blog/tech-packs/what-is-a-tech-pack/) lays out the basic sequence.

You'll move through five stages: Brief, Specify, Sample, Review and Approve. Your first job is to explain who the customer is, how much coverage you want and what the silhouette looks like. By the time the pack is finished, those choices need to be instructions the sample team can follow.

chart.alt: Workflow from a swimsuit brief to approved specifications
chart.caption: Move from decisions to an approved specification

body.text: In our scoop-back pack, the founder's fuller-seat reference became a marked back outline. The inside drawing tied LINING-SOFT to the lining panel and ELASTIC-LEG to the enclosed opening, with SHELL-NAVY on the exterior. Every component reference matched a swatch and a supplier entry in the materials table. When the technician asked, "How is the lining edge secured?", the answer became a construction decision instead of a comment nobody answered.

Set up that layout in an editable document with linked materials and measurement tables. Next to each measurement, enter the unit, the endpoints, whether it's relaxed or stretched, the target and the tolerance. Keep the intended body fit separate from the finished-garment dimensions. Make sure artwork placement and color references match across the drawings and attachments.

For our scoop-back material trial, we cut strips across the fabric and marked a 10 cm span. Each strip held a 500 g load for 30 seconds, then rested unloaded for 60 seconds. Dry, the shell stretched to 15 cm and the soft lining to 14 cm, and both came back to 10.1 cm. After a 10-minute soak in water, they stretched to 15.5 cm and 14.5 cm and came back to 10.2 cm. These were workshop comparisons for this material combination only.

Next, our patternmaker compared elastic cut lengths of 27 cm and 28 cm, each with the same 1 cm overlap, on the same leg-opening pattern with identical stitching. The shorter one pinched during movement, and the longer one stayed in place. The approved entry kept the 30 cm relaxed opening target and specified the longer elastic with the secured lining edge. Wet fit photos backed up that choice. The strip extension results alone didn't set the garment dimensions.

figure.alt: Technician holding a sewn swimwear edge trial at a sampling machine
figure.caption: A sewn edge trial tests the proposed construction

body.text: In the sample correction log, we changed the lining pattern and edge callout because the lining rolled outward. We kept the opening target and logged the buyer's later coverage request separately. That kept the reason for each revision clear.
Use the readiness matrix from earlier to manage open decisions. The worksheet below assumes a solid-color scoop-back with fuller coverage and individual bagging. Treat these as example inputs.

We quote before sampling. A quote can work from visible assumptions. Sampling needs agreed instructions, and bulk release needs accepted fit, materials, grading and packing. Before you export, cross-check the component references, drawing callouts and measurement rows. Date the PDF, keep its editable source, record the approval and note which version it replaces.

In our beginner trial, a founder who could sketch but had no patternmaking training spent 4 hours preparing this brief. They spent another 2 hours fixing undefined measurement endpoints and conflicting lining notes. The founder paid our USD 50 per-design fee, which included the tech pack and CAD pattern. Physical samples and courier delivery cost extra. The timed work covered preparing and correcting the document, not developing the sample.

Use that split to plan your own effort. You define the look and coverage, then bring in technical help for patterns, measurement methods and material trials. Keep in mind that the trial's timing applies only to that founder and that brief.

sections.heading: What does a clothing tech pack look like?

body.text: A clothing tech pack is a set of annotated garment drawings, materials and measurement tables, construction details and revision pages. You can expect front and back flat drawings, plus close-ups of details such as lining attachments. See [Shopify's How To Create a Tech Pack To Send To Manufacturers](https://www.shopify.com/blog/how-to-create-a-tech-pack).
Read across the pages and follow each component from its drawing callout to the bill of materials (BOM), the assembly instruction and the sample check. Here's that route through our scoop-back pack:

rows: SHELL-NAVY identifies the exterior; back outline shows fuller seat coverage
Compare neckline, scoop and seat with the drawings
LINING-SOFT matches the approved lining swatch; ELASTIC-LEG identifies the enclosed elastic
Turn the suit inside out to inspect the lining and opening
Turn and secure the lining edge; check the finished opening along the marked relaxed measurement path
Check the edge treatment separately from the opening measurement

body.text: The inside view shows the lining attachment, so you can compare it with the construction callout.

Remember the document map from the start: the measurement sheet sits inside the full pack. It doesn't supply the materials, construction and revision information around it, as [Techpacker's What Is a Tech Pack? The Complete Fashion Guide](https://techpacker.com/blog/tech-packs/what-is-a-tech-pack/) explains. Include the separate cutting pattern in the handover. A sketch shaped like a pattern only explains the pieces, unless it has been developed and verified for cutting.

Try this review exercise, which uses assumed entries for the same scoop-back style. Read the original entries before you check the answer key. The dimensions here are exercise inputs, not sizing rules.

columns: Corrected entry and approval before sampling
rows: Inside drawing: LINING-SOFT; BOM: firm lining
Use LINING-SOFT on both pages; brand approves the matching swatch
Strap detail: 10 mm elastic; BOM: 15 mm elastic
Use 10 mm elastic in both entries; technician confirms construction and brand approves strap appearance
Measurement row: "leg opening," with no method
Measure the full finished opening along its edge, relaxed, from the side seam back to that seam; technician marks the path and brand approves the method

body.text: To fix a contradiction, you have to remove the obsolete instruction everywhere it shows up. To fix an unanswered decision, you have to add an agreed instruction. Making the page look tidier fixes neither.
Our scoop-back revision record shows how that review carries on after sampling. These measurements apply to this style only.

rows: Initial pack named the lining but omitted its edge treatment
Sample opening measured 30 cm relaxed; lining rolled into view
Correct lining pattern and inside-view edge callout
Revised pattern and callout specified a turned, secured lining edge; measurement row retained the 30 cm target
Next sample measured 30.2 cm; lining stayed inside during wet movement

body.text: In our log, the later coverage request stayed a separate fit change. The cost section earlier covers the sample and courier charges for the lining correction.

Last, check what a template leaves out. [AI Techpacks' Fashion Tech Pack Template (Free Download + Checklist)](https://aitechpacks.com/blog/fashion-tech-pack-template) says its starter files don't include garment measurement charts, size grading or approved tolerances. Use the readiness worksheet above to close those fields before the relevant approval stage.
When you're ready to start your project, send us your references, intended sizes, fabric preferences and open questions. See our [Request a Quote](/request-a-quote/) page.
